turn_text: With regard to payment limits, Senator Grassley again wanted to see some change. The Senate plan was different than that of the House, the House a bit more liberal and who might be able to receive funds. How was it that the House bill or the House proposal made it to the final language?

Well, again, look at the situation we're in. In 1996, I was part of a very revolutionary farm bill called Freedom to Farm. somewhat controversial to say the least, but we changed this business farmers planning according to Washington as opposed to the market. That was key, but it was a tough sell. We didn't get it the first year. We got it in the next few months. This time we can't do that. We're in a very rough patch. So this is an evolutionary bill that is very predictable and it will enable our farmers and ranchers and and growers to go to their lenders and say, I'm good for the next five years. So it was a different circumstance with regard to payment limitations. There are a lot of folks in trouble, not only small farmers, not only small farming operations or specialty crops or whatever, but you have especially down south and out west where people are involved in lots of acres and a lot of expense. That whole operation may be very big to some people, But the other thing is that the Vietnam veterans who are farmers, they're getting up in years and they'd like to leave the farm if possible to that son or daughter. But maybe they don't want to do that. Maybe the son and daughter is gone. So we were worried about that. So now we have a cousin that maybe has been working the farm or a niece or a nephew. I think that's perfectly understandable in the dramatic situation that we find ourselves in with You've got to have access to technology and everything else. That's very costly. So a big operation can fail just as well as the small ones. So the payment limit reform that we did put in tried to address that issue.

turn_text: Is this an adequate bill for the day or again the best you could do?
It's both. It's the best we could do and I think it's adequate. I think it's a good bill.

The president has offered the market facilitation program to help soybean farmers and others who've been affected by trade, but has said there won't be any additional funds for 2019. Well, that would be what I call a mitigation payment. I guess you can call anything you want to. Farmers said at the beginning, and we also chimed in. The farmers don't want aid. They want trade. So progress in China, which I think is occurring, and China buying, not to the extent that they used to, but they need to step up. That helps our relationship with China. They become more dependent on us. It's a national security issue as well. That's all across the board. So if the administration focuses on restoring our trade relationships and recapturing our markets, there won't be any need for that. I mean, farmers are used to working with the market and the cycles that we experience. What they are not used to is the government intervening with tariff and then having a tariff retaliation. We'll be holding hearings on that in the coming year.

There were plenty of suggestions with regard to the conservation provisions and especially CRP. I think Mr. Peterson wanted to expand the acres and Senator Thune also wanted to look at a way that producers didn't have to go the full term with a contract. You did a little of both.

Yes, we tried to address that as best we could. We're very aware of Senator Thune's effort and, of course, Colin Piesen is a great friend. It's 27 million acres. So I think we did a pretty good job, given the circumstances we were in and the budget that we were in.

Thinking about the regional differences, I think it was Chairman Conway who wanted to look at some of those base acres that had been unplanted for a number of years and shift those dollars around. Yes, it did. Credit Chairman Conway for his effort. I was concerned that there is a tangible benefit with regards to acres that have not been tilled over a period of years and that the lender, if the fall of a sudden the farmer awakened to the fact after the farm bills passed and the FSA folks said, oh, by the way, those 10% of your ground is no longer in your acreage base. The person that would take real note of that would be the lender. And I don't know when the farmer goes in and talks to somebody, and you've seen a 10% loss in your acreage base, what happened? We tried to work with the USDA to predict exactly what happened, who would be hurt, where that would happen, most of it's in Texas, and a lot of it in Oklahoma, and a great deal of it in Kansas. So you had to figure out how many people would be harmed by this, as well as the trade-off of getting at least a CBO estimate on cost savings. I think we worked it out. I think we worked it out well to the best final product that we could.
